draft.title: Public goods
card: A public good has two features. It is non-rival: one person using it leaves no less for others. It is non-excludable: once it is provided, no one can be stopped from using it.
Examples include street lighting in a Melbourne suburb, flood defences along a Victorian river, national defence and lighthouses.
Because no one can be shut out, people can use the good without paying. This is the free rider problem. Firms cannot make people pay, so the market provides too little or none at all.
Most goods are private goods: rival and excludable. Some are partly public, such as a road, which can get crowded and can be tolled.
draft.remember: Non-rival and non-excludable, so free riders stop the market supplying it.

a.q: Why would a free market not supply enough street lighting for a Melbourne suburb?
opts: Residents can enjoy the light without paying
Street lights cost too much to install
Few residents in the suburb want street lighting
The council owns all the land in the suburb
a.why: Once a street light is on, everyone nearby can use it, whether they paid or not. People can free ride, so no firm can charge enough to cover the cost.
a.clue: Could a firm stop someone who did not pay from using the light?

b.q: A Victorian streaming service shows films to paying members only. One more viewer does not stop anyone else watching. Why is it not a public good?
opts: It is excludable
It is rival
It costs money to make
It is supplied by a private firm
b.why: Watching is non-rival, but people who do not pay can be shut out with a login. That makes it excludable, so the firm can charge and free riding is not a problem.
b.clue: Can people who do not pay be stopped?

a.best: Residents can enjoy the light without paying
